title: ECB leaks, CBC chains
summary: See ECB give away patterns byte by byte, then build CBC with an IV and PKCS#7 padding.

steps.title: ECB: each block on its own
body: **ECB** (Electronic Codebook) is the obvious mode: split the message into 16-byte blocks and encrypt each one separately with raw AES.
P1 ──AES──▶ C1     P2 ──AES──▶ C2     P3 ──AES──▶ C3

Because AES is deterministic, **equal plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks**. The famous picture is the "ECB penguin": a bitmap encrypted with ECB still shows the penguin, because every patch of one colour encrypts to the same bytes. In data it is just as bad: equal records, equal fields, a repeated header, all visible without the key.
ECB is never the right mode for data. It exists in the API because it is the raw primitive other modes are built from.

> **Fixed values for the exercises only.** The keys, IVs and nonces here are constants so the output is the same every run. Real code takes keys from `RandomNumberGenerator` or a key vault and never repeats a nonce with the same key.

steps.prompt: A 48-byte message is block A, block A again, then block B. What does this print?
code: aes.Key = new byte[16];                    // fixed for the demo
byte[] msg = Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes("PAY ALICE $100.0PAY ALICE $100.0PAY MALLORY $999");
steps.explain: Blocks 1 and 2 were equal in the plaintext, so they are equal in the ciphertext. An attacker sees the repetition, and could even cut and paste whole blocks to reorder a message.

steps.title: Detect ECB
prompt: ECB is detectable from the ciphertext alone: look for repeated 16-byte blocks.

Write `int RepeatedBlocks(byte[] cipher)` that splits `cipher` into 16-byte blocks and returns how many blocks are a repeat of an **earlier** block (three equal blocks count as 2 repeats). Assume the length is a multiple of 16.
template: Dojo.Eq("ECB of 3 equal blocks + 1 other has 2 repeats", 2, RepeatedBlocks(dojoEcb));
Dojo.Eq("CBC of the same message has none", 0, RepeatedBlocks(dojoCbc));
hints: Turn each block into a string with `Convert.ToHexString(cipher, i, 16)` and keep a `HashSet<string>`.
`HashSet.Add` returns false when the item was already there.

steps.title: CBC: chain the blocks
body: **CBC** (Cipher Block Chaining) XORs each plaintext block with the **previous ciphertext block** before encrypting it. The first block is XORed with an **IV** (initialisation vector), 16 bytes that must be **random and unpredictable for every message** and are sent in the clear next to the ciphertext.
C1 = AES(P1 ^ IV)     C2 = AES(P2 ^ C1)     C3 = AES(P3 ^ C2)
Equal blocks now encrypt differently, and the same message encrypted twice (with two IVs) looks unrelated.

CBC still only handles whole blocks, so it uses **PKCS#7 padding**: add `n` bytes each of value `n` to reach a multiple of 16. If the message already fills its last block, a whole extra block of sixteen `0x10` bytes is added, so padding can always be removed unambiguously.

code: byte[] iv = new byte[16];                  // fixed for the demo only
steps.explain: Padding always adds 1 to 16 bytes: 0 bytes becomes one block of padding, 15 gets 1 byte, 16 gets a full extra block, 20 rounds up to 32.
The IV is one block (16 bytes) whatever the key size, and decryption needs the same IV, which is why it is stored next to the ciphertext.

steps.prompt: A system uses AES-CBC with a key from a vault, but the IV is hard-coded to 16 zero bytes. What leaks?
options: Whether two messages are equal, or start with the same blocks
Nothing, since the IV is not secret anyway
steps.explain: With a fixed IV, CBC becomes deterministic again: equal messages give equal ciphertexts, and equal prefixes give equal leading blocks. The IV is not secret, but it must be fresh and unpredictable.

steps.prompt: Arrange the body of a hand-written CBC encryption loop for one block.
steps.explain: XOR with the previous ciphertext block (the IV the first time), encrypt, emit, and remember the result for the next block.

steps.title: CBC by hand
prompt: Write `byte[] CbcEncrypt(byte[] key, byte[] iv, byte[] plain)` using only raw AES on single blocks (`EncryptEcb` with `PaddingMode.None`) and XOR. Assume `plain.Length` is a multiple of 16 (no padding yet).
The tests compare your output byte for byte with .NET's own `EncryptCbc(plain, iv, PaddingMode.None)`, so your chaining must be exactly right.
starter: byte[] CbcEncrypt(byte[] key, byte[] iv, byte[] plain)
solution: byte[] CbcEncrypt(byte[] key, byte[] iv, byte[] plain)
template: var dojoPlain = System.Text.Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes("same block here!same block here!and a third one..");
Dojo.Check("equal plaintext blocks now encrypt differently", !dojoMine[0..16].SequenceEqual(dojoMine[16..32]), "blocks 1 and 2 are equal");

Dojo.Eq("one block works too", Convert.ToHexStringLower(dojoAes.EncryptCbc(new byte[16], dojoIv, System.Security.Cryptography.PaddingMode.None)), Convert.ToHexStringLower(CbcEncrypt(dojoKey, dojoIv, new byte[16])));
hints: Keep a `previous` array that starts as the IV.
For each block: XOR with `previous`, `EncryptEcb(mixed, PaddingMode.None)`, copy into the output, then `previous = c`.

steps.title: PKCS#7 padding by hand
prompt: Write `byte[] Pad(byte[] data)` and `byte[] Unpad(byte[] data)` for 16-byte blocks:
- `Pad` adds `n = 16 - data.Length % 16` bytes, each of value `n` (so 1 to 16 bytes, never 0).

- `Unpad` reads the last byte `n`, checks that `n` is 1 to 16, that the data is a non-empty multiple of 16, and that the last `n` bytes all equal `n`; otherwise it throws `CryptographicException`. Then it returns the data without them.
That "is the padding valid?" check is exactly what a padding oracle attack abuses, as you will see in lesson 5.
solution: for (int i = data.Length; i < result.Length; i++)
if (data.Length == 0 || data.Length % 16 != 0) throw new CryptographicException("Bad length.");
if (n < 1 || n > 16) throw new CryptographicException("Bad padding.");
for (int i = data.Length - n; i < data.Length; i++)
if (data[i] != n) throw new CryptographicException("Bad padding.");
template: Dojo.Eq("Pad(5 bytes) adds eleven 0x0b", "01020304050b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b", Convert.ToHexStringLower(Pad(new byte[] { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 })));
Dojo.Eq("Pad(16 bytes) adds a whole block", 32, Pad(new byte[16]).Length);
Dojo.Eq("the extra block is sixteen 0x10", Enumerable.Repeat((byte)16, 16).ToArray(), Pad(new byte[16])[16..]);
Dojo.Eq("Pad(empty) is one block of 0x10", 16, Pad(Array.Empty<byte>()).Length);
Dojo.Eq("same padding as .NET's PKCS7", Convert.ToHexStringLower(dojoAes.EncryptCbc(dojoData, new byte[16], System.Security.Cryptography.PaddingMode.PKCS7)),
Dojo.Throws<System.Security.Cryptography.CryptographicException>("a length that is not a multiple of 16 is rejected", () => Unpad(new byte[] { 1 }));
hints: `int n = 16 - data.Length % 16;` is always between 1 and 16.
In `Unpad`, `data[^1]` is the last byte and `data[..^n]` drops the last `n`.
